title: Introduction and Character of the Nimbarka Sampradaya
summary: Introduction and Character of the Nimbarka Sampradaya — A source-conscious study of this subject.
body:
The Nimbarka Sampradaya is a distinct Vaishnava lineage whose philosophical teaching is known as Dvaitadvaita Vedanta. Its understanding of the relationship between the Supreme, the individual self and the world is closely connected with devotion to Bhagavan, reverence for the Guru, and the worship of Shri Radha-Krishna. A meaningful introduction therefore requires more than a list of historical names: it calls for a coordinated study of its object of worship, philosophy, spiritual discipline, texts and teacher-disciple lineage.

## The object of worship and devotion

The worship of Shri Radha-Krishna Yugala holds a central place in the Nimbarka tradition. Devotional practice includes loving dedication to Bhagavan, surrender, service to the Guru, mantra and name repetition, meditation and worshipful service. Initiation and guidance within the lineage are traditionally important; discussions of mantras and esoteric worship should therefore respect authoritative ritual manuals and the discipline of the tradition.

## The relationship between philosophy and practice

Dvaitadvaita Vedanta presents difference and non-difference together. It does not regard the individual self and the world as wholly independent of Brahman, nor does it erase their distinct identity and experienced differences. In spiritual practice, the self, dependent upon the Supreme, advances through devotion, surrender and service to Bhagavan.

## A method for study

A reliable study of the sampradaya should draw upon primary works of the Acharyas, commentaries, sub-commentaries, ritual manuals, institutional records and available historical materials. Traditional narratives should be identified as accounts preserved by the lineage, while inscriptions, manuscripts and documentary records should be treated as historical evidence. This distinction allows both devotion and research to be respected.

Editorial note: This is an introductory account of the broad doctrinal character of the sampradaya. Specific historical claims, dates and questions of authorship require separate source-based examination.
